# Ibn Ezra on Exodus

אבן עזרא על שמות

Link: [https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus)

פירוש פשט המשלב ביאורים המבוססים על דקדוק ובלשנות; חובר במאה ה-12.

12th-century commentary focusing on the simple meaning of the text and incorporating grammar and linguistics.

Sections: Chapter-Verse-Comment

Location: Tanakh/Rishonim on Tanakh/Ibn Ezra/Torah

Originally from [Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org) via [TorahLM.org](https://torahlm.org) — see [licensing](https://torahlm.org/sefaria_license).

Version (En): Ibn Ezra's commentary on the Pentateuch, tran. and annot. by H. Norman Strickman and Arthur M. Silver. Menorah Pub., 1988-2004 (Segments: 1652)


## Chapter 1


### Verse 1

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:1:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:1)


ספר ואלה שמות, חבור לאברהם נשלם שנת תתקי"ג יקר כמו שהם


May the writer and the reader be strong and steadfast¹ 38. The printed editions omit it as they do many of the other poems which introduce Torah portions in I.E.’s *Commentary* on Exodus. Some manuscripts open with the following introduction: Abraham’s commentary on the book of Exodus, finished in the year 4913 (1152-53 C.E.), is as precious as onyx. However, other commentaries give the date 4927 (1166-67 C.E.) as the date of the manuscript’s completion. E. Levine notes, “Some writers have held that the 1152-53 date refers to the long commentary whereas the inscription 1166-67 refers to the short commentary; others have maintained that the 1152-53 refers to the short commentary and the 1166-67 refers to the long commentary which was written precisely between 1159 and 1167 C.E.” See Foreword. in the very ark². The reference is to I.E.’s commentary on Exodus. Commenting on the word *ba-aron* (in a coffin) in Gen. 50:26, I.E. explains, “The reason why *ba-aron* is vocalized with a *kamatz* is that it signifies the coffin which he had prepared for himself.” (See notes on Gen. 50:26.) The word *aron* can refer to an ark or to a coffin. I.E. is being a bit morbid. which is the house which the author prepared for himself.I now begin to explain the Torah portion, *Shemot;* which opens the second Book of the Torah.

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:1:2

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:2](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:2)


**ואלה,** טעם הוי"ו בעבור שהזכיר בסוף הספר הראשון, כי ראה יוסף לבניו בני שלשים (ברא' נ כב) הזכיר כי אחיו ברדתם היו מעטים ופרו ורבו ומלת אלה גם בחסרון הה"א שוה לזכרים ולנקבות וכתיב "כי את כל התועבות האל" (ויקרא יח כז) ואחריו מכל התועבות האלה (שם שם כט), לאנשים האל (ברא' יט ח) אלה ילדו להרפה (ש"ב כא כב) מה אעשה לאלה (ברא' לא מג) וככה מלת לז, השונמית הלז (מ"ב ד כה) הנער הלז (זכרי' ב ה), ובעבור היות מלת אלה מלעיל היה הה"א נוסף כה"א לילה (ברא' א ה) נחלה מצרים (במד' לד ה), ושם לשון זכר ורבים שמות כי התי"ו כולל סימן רבים ורבות כמו מקומות ואבות, גם המ"ם ככה סימן הזכרים והנקבות, כמו נשים ופלגשים ויש שמות שימצאו במ"ם גם בתי"ו כמו נפשים (יחז' יג כ) נפשות (שם שם יח) לבבות (דה"א כח ט) גם לבבים על לבבהן (נחום ב ה):


NOW THESE ARE. Our book opens with a *vav*³ which literally means, and these are, and is so translated by I.E. The question thus arises, why open a book with a connective? Indeed, Deut. 1:1 opens with *elleh ha-devarim* and not with *ve-elleh ha-devarim*. Similarly, Exodus should have read *elleh shemot* and not *ve-elleh shemot*. because the end of Genesis relates that *Joseph saw the children of the third generation* (Genesis 50:23).⁴, i.e., that he was fruitful. However, it does not tell us about the fate of his brothers. The latter is related to us at the beginning of Exodus where we are told that *the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly* (Ex. 1:7). Thus the opening part of Exodus is connected to the closing section of Genesis. Hence the connective *vav*. Scripture notes that Joseph’s brothers were few in number when they descended to Egypt but that they were fruitful and multiplied there (Exodus 1:7).The word *elleh* (these) and *el* (these) are employed equally with the masculine and the feminine. We thus find, *For all these abominations* (ha-to’evot ha-el)⁵ (abominations) is feminine. (Leviticus 18:27) and then afterward, *any of these abominations* (ha-to’evot ha-elleh) (Lev. 18:29). We similarly read, *unto these men* (la-anashim ha-el) (Gen. 19:8); *These four* (arba’at elleh) *were born to the giant* (II Samuel 21:22); *and what can I do this day for these* (la-elleh) *my daughters* (Gen. 31:43). The same is the case with the word *laz* (that one).⁶ We thus find, *that Shunamite* (ha-shunammit ha-laz) (II Kings 4:25) and *this young man* (ha-na’ar ha-laz) (Zechariah 2:8). The fact that the word *elleh* is penultimately accented indicates that its *heh* is superfluous.⁷. The *heh* added to the word has no meaning. It is like the *heh* of *laylah* (night)⁸. and the *heh* of *nachlah* (brook) in *the Brook of* (nachlah) *Egypt* (Numbers 34:5).⁹.

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:1:3

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:3](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:3)


ה"א מצרימה, תחת מלת "אל" כמו נלכה דותינה (ברא' לז יז) ותבא אותי ירושלימה (יחז' ח ג):


[THE NAMES OF.] *Shem* (name) is masculine. Its plural form is *shemot* (names), for the *tav* is used for both the masculine and the feminine.¹⁰ can be a plural masculine. I.E. makes this point because generally speaking only feminine plurals end in a *tav*. Compare, *mekomot* (places)¹¹, which is masculine. and *avot* (fathers). The *mem* is similarly used as a masculine and feminine plural. Compare, *nashim* (women) and *pilagshim* (concubines).¹² We also find some nouns employing both the *tav* and the *mem* in the plural forms. Compare, *nefashim* (souls) (Ezekiel 13:20) and *nefashot* (souls)¹³ is feminine. (Ezek. 13:18). We similarly find, *levavot* (hearts) (II Chronicles 28:9) and *levavim* (hearts).¹⁴ (heart) is masculine. Compare, *al livvehen* (upon their hearts)¹⁵ is made up of the plural *levavim* plus the suffix for their. (Nahum 2:8).[Into Egypt.] The *heh* of *mitzrayemah* (into Egypt) is in place of the word *el* (to). Compare, *dotayenah* (to Dothan) in *nelekh dotayenah* (let us go down to Dothan) (Gen. 37:16); and *yerushalayemah* (to Jerusalem) in *and brought me in the vision of God to Jerusalem* (Ezek. 8:3).¹⁶ is equivalent to *el yerushalayim* (to Jerusalem) and *dotayenah* to *el dotan* (to Dothan). Similarly, *mitzrayemah* is equivalent to *el mitzrayim* (to Egypt).

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:1:4

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:4](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:4)


**את יעקב.** עם יעקב כמו כרת ד' את אברם (ברא' טו יח):


WITH JACOB. *Et ya’akov* means with Jacob.¹⁷ is usually placed before the direct object. Here it is used as a preposition meaning with. Compare, *In that day the Lord made a covenant with* (et) *Abram* (Gen. 15:18).

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:1:5

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:5](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:1:5)


**איש וביתו.** יוצאי חלצו ואין בית בכל המקרא אשה, והנה העד איש וביתו באו, כי לא היו נשי השבטים במספר השבעים, ואל יקשה בעיניך וכפר בעדו ובעד ביתו (ויקרא טז, ו, יא) כי פשוטו בית אביו, כי שלשה וידוין היו ועזר הכהן שהיא אשתו בכח בעדו, והיא נכללת עמו, כי האיש ואשתו הוא האדם:


EVERY MAN CAME WITH HIS HOUSEHOLD. *Beto* (his household) refers to those who came out of his loins. The term *bayit* (house, household) in Scripture never refers to a wife.¹⁸ (house) as a synonym for wife. Cf. *Sabbath* 118b: “Rabbi Jose said, I never called my wife, my wife but I called her my house.” Also see *Yoma* 2a, “*Beto zo ishto* (*His household* [Lev. 16:18] refers to his wife).” *Every man came with his household* (beto) is proof of this, for the wives of the tribes are not included in the seventy who descended into Egypt.¹⁹ does not mean one’s wife. Do not permit the verse *and* (the high priest shall) *have made atonement for himself, and for his household* (beto) (Lev. 16:18) to cause you any difficulty.²⁰, “his household” seems to refer to the wife of the high priest. See end of note 18. For according to the plain meaning of the text, *beto* (his household) refers to his father’s house. *Beto* (his household) must be so interpreted because the high priest made three confessions on the Day of Atonement.²¹ (Lev. 16:18). According to the Talmud the making of atonement refers to confession of sins (*viduy*). Cf. *Yoma* 36b. The three confessions offered by the high priest were on behalf of himself (*for himself*), on behalf of the house of Aaron (*his household*), and on behalf of the people of Israel (*and for all the assembly of Israel*). The priest’s helpmate, who is his wife, is included in the term *for himself*. She is included with him because a husband and a wife make a “man.”²² 63a: “Any Jew that has no wife is not a man.” Also see Gen. 1:27, *And God created man…male and female created He them*.

### Verse 2

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:2:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:2:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:2:1)


**ראובן. ויהודה** כל שהוא נע כזי"ן זבולן בהכנס עליו אחת מאותיות בוכ"ל וראוי להיות האות המשרת בשוא נע, והנה אין יכולת בלשון לקרוא שני שואין נעים, על כן שמו חירק תחת האות המשרת, כי אז היה בי"ת האות המשרת הנכנס עליו יאמרו בִּזבולן, ואם כ"ף או למ"ד כִּזבולן, לִזבולן, ואם וי"ו יאמרו שורק תחת חירק, כאלו הוי"ו בקריאת אלף, כמו וזבולן, כי המלה תראה כקריאת אל"ף או זבולן, ואם היה האות הראשון יו"ד כמו יהודה, שהיו"ד מאותיות הנעלמות יעלימוהו, כמו נעלה ביהודה (ישעי' ז' ו') כִיהודה ליהודה נחשון (במד' א ז), כי עתה היו"ד הוא נעלם, ואינו נזכר ונרגש בשפה, וגם ככה עם וי"ו ויהודה, והנה נכתבו השבטים הנה כסדר תולדותם:


REUBEN. When a word beginning with a letter that is vocalized with a mobile *sheva* (*sheva na*), e.g., the *zayin* of Zevulun, has a *bet, vav, kaf*, or *lamed* prefixed to it, the prefix ideally should also be vocalized with a mobile *sheva*.²³, and *lamed* are prepositional prefixes. They are usually vocalized with a mobile *sheva*. I.E. explains the rules of the vocalization of the prefixes in this note because a connective *vav* is prefixed to many of the names of the sons of Jacob listed in our chapter. However, due to the impossibility of sounding two mobile *sheva’im* in succession these prefixes are vocalized with a *chirik* rather than with a *sheva*. Hence if the word *zevulun* has a *bet* prefixed to it we say *bi-zevulun* (in Zebulun), If *zevulun* has a *kaf* or *lamed* prefixed to it we say *ki-zevulun* (like Zebulun) or *li-zevulun* (to Zebulun). However, if the word has a *vav* prefixed to it then it is vocalized with a *shuruk* rather than a *chirik*. We sound the *vav* as if it had an *alef* preceding it and pronounce the word *u-zevulun* (and Zebulun) for the word is sounded as if it were written *alef vav* plus *zevulun*.²⁴ is the sign of the *shuruk*. I.E. explains that a *shuruk* is sounded as if spelled *alef vav;* i.e., it is pronounced ooh. However, if we deal with a word whose first letter is a *yod*, an example being the name *yehudah*, then the *yod* is silent, for the *yod* is one of the quiescent letters.²⁵, and *yod*. These letters surrender their consonantal function by coalescing with surrounding vowel signs at the end of a syllable or word. Thus the *yod* following a *chirik* or *tzere* is not sounded as a consonant. Hence the term quiescent letters. Compare, *biyhudah* (against Judah) in *Let us go up against Judah* (Isaiah 7:6) and *kiyhudah* (like Judah) and *liyhudah* (of Judah) in *Of Judah, Nahshon* (Num. 1:7). In the latter case the *yod* is silent and is not perceived or felt when the word is enunciated. The same is also the case when a *vav* is prefixed to the word *yehudah*. The word is pronounced *viyhudah*.The tribes are here listed in order of their births.²⁶

footnotes:
²³ The bet, vav, kaf
²⁴ Vav
²⁵ The quiescent letters are the alef, heh, vav
²⁶ In the order in which they were born to their mothers. First Leah’s children are listed in the order of their birth. Then Rachel’s son Benjamin is listed. The children of the wives are followed by the children of the handmaids. The latter are also listed in the order that their mothers bore them. Joseph is listed last because he was in Egypt when the others arrived there (Krinsky).



### Verse 3

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:3:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:3:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:3:1)


**יששכר.** בעבור התחברות שני שיני"ן חסרו האחר מהמבטא כדרך מחצצרים (דה"א טו כד) שיקרא מחצרים ואין שי"ן כמוה במקרא ומנהג העברים בהתחבר וי"ו עם אחד מאותיות השפה שהם במ"פ חבירי הוי"ו ינעו אל"ף נוסף בקריאה וינקדו הוי"ו בשורק כמו ופרו ורבו (ירמי' כנ ג) ומלאו בתי מצרים (למטה ח יז) וככה ובנימין, בעבור היות בנימין בן הגברת הזכירו לפני בני השפחות:


ISSACHAR. Because the two *sins* in *yissachar* (Issachar) are written in succession only one is sounded. Compare, the word *machtzetzrim* (did blow) (I Chron. 15:24), which is pronounced *machtzerim*.²⁷ in succession. However, only one *tzadi* is sounded. Similarly, *yissachar* is pronounced *yisachar*. We do not find a similar case with regard to the *sin* in Scripture.²⁸ are written in succession and only one is pronounced (Krinsky). It is customary for the Hebrews to pronounce a *vav* prefixed to the labials which are related to the *vav*, namely, the *bet, mem, peh* with an *alef* added to it,²⁹ is a labial. Before a labial the *vav* is not pronounced like a labial but is pronounced “ooh” so as not to have two labials back to back. and to vocalize the *vav* with a *shuruk*. Compare, *u-faru* (and they shall be fruitful) in *and they shall be fruitful and multiply* (Jeremiah 23:3); and *u-male’u* (shall be full) in *and the houses of the Egyptians shall he full of swarms of flies* (Ex. 8:17). The word *u-vinyamin* (and Benjamin) is similar. Benjamin is listed before the children of the handmaidens³⁰ because he was a son of one of Jacob’s wives.

### Verse 4

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:4:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:4:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:4:1)


**דן.** בהתחבר השמות הם על ששה דרכים, נכונים, האחד כמו עילם ואשור וארפכשד (ברא' י כב) והשני בנפך ארגמן ורקמה ובוץ (יחז' כז טז) השלישי אודם פטדה וברקת (למטה כח יז) הרביעי דן ונפתלי גד ואשר החמישי מור ואהלות קציעות (תה' מה ט) הששי אדם שת אנוש (דה"א א א):


DAN. Names are connected to each other in Scripture in six different ways. All of these styles are correct. One way of listing names is, *Elam, and Asshur, and Arpachshad* (Gen. 10:22).³¹ (and) is placed before each of the names that follows the first name (Krinsky). A second manner is, *with carbuncles, purple, and richly woven work, and fine linen* (Ezek. 27:16).³² is placed after the first two names in a list. A third way is, *carnelian, topaz, and smaragd* (Ex. 28:17).³³ is placed before the last name in the list. A fourth way is, *Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher*.³⁴ is placed before each of the second names in a list. The fifth is, *Myrrh, and aloes, and cassia* (Psalms 45:9).³⁵ is omitted before the last name. The verse literally reads, *Myrrh, and aloes, cassia are all thy garments*. The sixth way is, *Adam, Seth, Enosh* (I Chron. 1:1).³⁶ is employed.

### Verse 5

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:5:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:5:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:5:1)


**ויהי.,** מלת יהי, היתה ראויה להיות כמו ירב המשא עליו (דה"ב כד כז), ובעבור היות הה"א מן הגרון פתחו במלת יהי, היו"ד הראשונה בקמץ קטן יֶהִי, והיה ראוי להיות היו"ד האחרון בשוא נח נראה, כמו הבי"ת במלת ירב והיה ראוי להיות יהי רק יכבד על הלשון על כן העלימוהו וננקד הה"א בחירק על כן "לו יְהִי" (ברא' ל לד) "כי הוא אמר וַיֶהִי" (תה' לג ט), ובעבור שידברו במלה הזאת הרבה תמיד, השיבו הטעם מלרע, והניעו היו"ד בשו"א, יהי כן ד' (למטה י י), על כן אין בבנין הקל פעל שיהיה האות המשרת בשוא, רק זאת הגזרה וגזרת ויחי יעקב (ברא' מז כח) והיה זה כי השתים האותיות שלו שרש מאלה השתי גזירות ויהי ויחי, השתי אותיות הם מאותיות הנוח, והם יו"ד ה"א היה, חיה, ובעבור כי אלה שתי האותיות הם מאותיות הנוח, פעמים שאינם נראים בסוף המלה בא האות המשרת שהוא היו"ד עליהם בשוא, ולא כן בכל הגזרות בבנין הקל:


WERE. The word *yehi* (let it be)³⁷ (were) is the word *yehi* with a conversive *vav*. should have been vocalized like the word *yirev* (the multitude)³⁸ is conjugated in the shortened third person imperfect *kal* form, the *yod* prefix is vocalized with a *chirik* and the first root letter with a *segol*. Compare, *yiven* (he will build), *yigel* (he will uncover). Thus *yehi* should have been vocalized *yihey*. in *and the multitude of the burdens against him* (II Chron. 24:27). However, since the *heh* is a guttural, the word *yehi* is vocalized with a *segol*³⁹ beneath the first *yod* and the word is read *yehi*. Furthermore, the final *yod* of *yehi* should have been pronounced with a sounded *sheva nach* (a quiescent *sheva*) as is the case with the word *yirev*. The word should thus have been pronounced *yihey*. However, because of the difficulty involved in the enunciation of the word in the aforementioned manner, the *yod*⁴⁰. was silenced and we vocalized the *heh* with a *chirik*. Hence the word is pronounced *yehi* (*sheva* beneath the *yod*) as in, *Behold, would it might be* (yehi) *according to thy word* (Gen. 30:34), or *yehi* (*segol* beneath the *yod*), as in *For He spoke, and it was* (va-yehi) (Ps. 33:9). The accent is placed on the last syllable of *yehi* and a *sheva* is placed beneath its *yod*⁴¹ prefix. because the word is used often in conversation, as in *So be* (yehi khen) *the Lord* (Ex. 10:10). Therefore only this root and the root of *va-yechi* in *And Jacob lived*⁴². (Gen. 47: 28) are found to have an imperfect *yod* prefix vocalized with a *sheva*⁴³ prefix is usually vocalized with a *chirik* in the *kal*. when conjugated in the *kal*. The reason for this is that two letters of the two roots *va-yechi* and *va-yehi* consist of the quiescent letters *yod, heh*, the root of one being *heh, yod, heh* and that of the other *chet, yod, heh*. Now since the *yod* and the *heh* are quiescent letters and are at times not pronounced at the end of a word, the *yod* prefix is vocalized with a *shev*a. We do not find any such other case in the *kal*.

⁴² From the root chet, yod, heh
⁴³ An imperfect yod

AND INCREASED ABUNDANTLY. *Va-yishretzu* (and increased abundantly) is similar to the word *yishretzu* (swarm) in *Let the waters swarm* (yishretzu) (Gen. 1:20). However, in the first instance⁵⁸ in our verse. the verb is independent.⁵⁹ It is like the verbs went, sat, stood, and lay. In the second instance⁶⁰ in Gen. 1:20. the verb is dependent upon something else. It is like the verbs ate, kept, and hired. We thus say, he ate the bread, he kept the thing, and he hired the donkey. The latter are called transitive verbs. Now *yishretzu* (swarm) in *yishretzu ha-mayim* (Let the waters swarm) is a transitive verb, while *va-yishretzu* (and increased abundantly) is an intransitive verb. Thus the root *shin, resh, zadi* is sometimes transitive and sometimes intransitive. It is like the root of the word *shav*⁶¹. which is at times intransitive as in *and (God) will return* (ve-shav) *and gather* (Deut. 30:3) and at times transitive, as in *that then the Lord thy God will turn* (ve-shav) *thy captivity* (*Ibid.*). It is possible that the word *va-yishretzu* alludes to the fact that the Israelite wives gave birth to twins and even more.⁶² is *shin, resh, zadi* our verse is to be rendered, the children of Israel swarmed (*va-yishretzu*); i.e., they multiplied like insects. See also Rashi, quoting *Shemot Rabbah*, that they bore six children at each birth. I myself have seen the quadruplets that a women gave birth to. Physicians tell us that a woman can have as many as seven fetuses in her womb at one time.

FOR US. When the word *mi-mennu* (for us) is in the plural⁷⁶ may mean from him or from us (of us). the books of the Babylonians⁷⁷ adhere to the grammatical rule⁷⁸, meaning us, is added to a verb in the plural no *dagesh* is placed in the *nun*. Compare, *shamarnu* (we kept), and *katavnu* (we wrote) (Filwarg). and always omit the *dagesh* in the *nun* in order to differentiate between *mi-mennu* in the plural and *mi-mennu* in *Out of him*⁷⁹. (mi-mennu) *shall come forth the cornerstone* (Zech. 10:4). In the latter, *nu* is a third person singular suffix and has a *dagesh* placed in the *nun* in accordance with the grammatical rule.⁸⁰ signifying the third person singular always receives a *dagesh*. Compare, *yishmerenno* (Filwarg). However, all the books coming out of the Land of Israel⁸¹ have a *dagesh* in the *nun* of *mi-mennu* both in the singular and in the plural because the *nun* of *mi-menni* (from me)⁸². This appears to be a scribal error. It is clear from the context that we should read *mi-menni* (Filwarg, Krinsky). I.E.’s point is that *mi-mennu* in the plural receives a *dagesh* despite the rule because *mi-menni* in the singular also should not have received a *dagesh*. in the singular has a *dagesh* despite the rule.⁸³ generally does not receive a *dagesh*. For the *nuns* of *ani* (I) and *necheni* (hath led me) in *the Lord hath led me* (Gen. 24:27)⁸⁴ of the first person suffix (*ni*) does not receive a *dagesh*. do not receive a *dagesh*.Now the word *min* (from) is doubled,⁸⁵ (from me) is a contraction of *min min ni* (from from me). the *nun* of *mi-menni* receives a *dagesh* to make up for the missing *nun* of the second *min*, and the word is read as if written *mi-menni*. The *nun* of the first *min* is represented by the *dagesh* in the second *mem* of *mi-menni*⁸⁶ in the second *mem* of *mi-menni* and the word is therefore pronounced *mi-mmenni*. The *mem* is doubled to make up for the missing *nun* of the first *min*. See previous note. and the *nun* of the suffix *ni* serves as if it were in the place of the one speaking.⁸⁷ Similarly, the *nun* of *mi-munnu* in the plural, spelled *mem mem nun nun vav* (Gen. 23:6), receives a *dagesh* and is read as if written *mi-mennu*.⁸⁸ in *mi-mennu* in the plural is the same as that of *mi-menni*. The first *dagesh* (in the second *mem*) compensates for the missing *nun* of the first *min*, and the second one (in the *nun*) compensates for the missing *nun* of the second *min*. For *mi-mennu* is a compound of *min min nu* (*nu* being short for *anachnu*) in the same way that *mi-menni* is short for *min min ni*. The reason that the *nun* of *mi-mennu* (of him) in the singular receives a *dagesh* is to compensate for the swallowed *heh*,⁸⁹ (*heh, vav*) is the usual third person suffix. This suffix is missing in *mi-mennu* (of him). The *dagesh* in the *nun* compensates for the missing *heh*. for it is only in a few instances when the verb *yishmor* (he will keep) is combined with a third person suffix that we say *yishmero* (he will keep him). The same is true of the word *yikre’o* (he shall be called) in *whereby he shall be called* (Jer. 23:6) and the word *yirdefo* (shall pursue him) in *The enemy shall purse him* (Hosea 8:3). The usual form of the third person suffix is *yishmerehu* (preserve him) (Ps. 41:8). Thus *yishmero* (he will keep him) is a shortened form. It is similar to *hinnehu* in *and, behold, he* (ve-hinnehu) *was at his work* (Jer. 18:3), in which *hinnehu* is a compound of *hinneh* (behold) and *hu* (he); and to *ve-hinneh nitzav* (and, lo he stood) (Num. 23:6).⁹⁰ is the long form. *Ve-hinneh* is the short form, for *ve-hinneh nitzav* is short for *ve-hinnehu nitzav*. At other times an additional *nun* is added,⁹¹ rather than one *nun* are suffixed to a verb ending in a first person pronoun. as in *yeshacharuneni* (they will seek me earnestly) and *yimtza’uneni* (they will find me) in *They will seek me earnestly, but they shall not find me* (Proverbs 1:28). Similarly, the word *tevarakhani* (may bless me) in *that thy soul may bless me* (Gen. 27:19) is pronounced *tevarekhanni* because of the *dagesh* in the *nun*.⁹² doubles the *nun*. We also find an extra *nun* in the word *yekhabbdaneni* (honoreth Me) in *whoso offereth the sacrifice of thanksgiving honoreth Me* (Ps. 50:23) and in the words *yesovavenhu* (He compassed him about), *yevonanehu* (He cared for him), and *yitzrenhu* (He kept him) (Deut. 32:10).⁹³ At other times the third person *heh* suffix is swallowed by the *nun*, as in *yishmerennu*⁹⁴ is doubled to compensate for the missing *heh*. (kept it in) in *and its owner hath not kept it in* (Ex. 21:29).

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:10:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:10:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:10:1)


**הבה.** הבה את אשתי (ברא' כט כא) לשון זכר, והוא הנכון כמו לכה נא עמנו ולנקבה הבי המטפחת (רות ג' טו), לכי ובאי (מ"א א יג), בעבור שידברו במלות האלה הרבה, יאמרו הבה נרדה (ברא' יא) ולנקבה הבה נא אבוא אליך (שם לח טז) כמו "לכה נשקה את אבינו יין" (שם יט לב):


COME (HAVAH). The word *havah* (give) in *Give me my wife* (Gen. 29:21) is in the masculine and as such is properly used there.⁹⁵, which is a masculine singular imperative, is properly used. J.P.S. in our verse translates *havah* as come. It is similar to the word *lekhah* (come) in *come, I pray thee with us*.⁹⁶. I.E.’s point is that both *havah* and *lekhah* come from stems that have a *yod* as their first letter and a *heh* added to their roots in the masculine singular imperative form; i.e., at times we say *havah* and *lekhah* in place of *hav* and *lekh*. In the feminine we say *havi*, as in *Bring* (havi) *the mantle that is upon thee* (Ruth 3:15), and *lekhi* (go), as in *Go and get thee in* (I Kings 1:23). Now because these words are used often the masculine form is employed both as a plural and as a feminine singular.⁹⁷ is a masculine singular form. Nevertheless, it is also used when the rules of grammar call for *havu* (in the plural) or *havi* (in the feminine singular). Scripture thus reads, *Come* (havah), *let us go down* (Gen. 11:7);⁹⁸ is used as a plural. *Come* (havah) *I Pray thee, let me come in unto thee* (Gen. 38:16).⁹⁹ is here employed as a feminine. It is like *Come* (lekhah), *let us make our father drink wine* (Gen. 19:32).¹⁰⁰ is used as a feminine. The usual feminine form of this word is *lekhi. Lekhah* is ordinarily masculine.

לו. בעבורו, כמו "אמרי לי" (שם כ יג), דע, כי כל הפעלים עוברים או עתידים שם הפועל בכחם, פי' שם דבר הנגזר מן הפועל שהוא חסר הוא נשמע מכח הפעלים כמו "והנה ברכת ברך" (במד' כג יא) "וברך ולא אשיבנה" (שם שם כ) והטעם וברך ברכה, וככה "וברוב יועצים תקום" (משלי טו כב), והשלם יועצים עצה תקום, וככה כי תקראנה קורות מלחמה, א"ר מרינוס, כי טעם ועלה מן הארץ, כמו ועלינו, ודבר ככה שלא יכשיל השטן פיהו, ולפי דעתי אין צורך.


WITH THEM. The word *lo* (with them) is to be rendered, because of them.¹⁰² (with them) is, to him. Hence I.E.’s comment. It is similar to the word *li* (of me) in *say of me* (Gen. 20:13).¹⁰³Note that all perfect and imperfect verbs imply a verbal noun.¹⁰⁴. I.E. uses this term for both a noun and an infinitive (Weiser). I.E.’s point is that there are instances in which a noun or an infinitive should follow a verb but it does not. In other words, even though a noun derived from a verb is missing in the text it is implied in the verb. For example, *ve-hinneh berakhta varekh* (and, behold, thou hast blessed them altogether) (Num. 23:11)¹⁰⁵ (in this case the infinitive) *barekh* is stated in the text. and *And when He hath blessed, I cannot call it back* (Num. 23:20), the meaning of which is: And when he hath blessed a blessing, I cannot call it back.¹⁰⁶ (blessing) is omitted from the text. However, it is implied by the verb *u-verakh* (and when he hath blessed). The same is true of *But in the multitude of counsellors they are established* (Prov. 15:22). The complete version of the latter is: But in the multitude of counsellors, counsel is established.¹⁰⁷ (counsel) was stated rather than implied in the word *yo’atzim* (counsellors). Similarly, *when there befalleth us any war* (v. 10) is to be interpreted as, when there befalleth us any accidents of war.¹⁰⁸ (there befalleth) is a plural. *Milchamah* (war) is a singular. Hence I.E. suggests that the verse be read as if the noun *korot* (accidents) were written between *tikrenah* and *milchamah*.Rabbi Merinus¹⁰⁹ says that *and get them out of the land* means, and we will get us out of the land. He believes that Pharaoh said *and get them out of the land* so that Satan would not ensnare him in the utterances of his mouth.¹¹⁰ 11a and Rashi on this verse. However, I see no need for this interpretation.¹¹¹ means: Israel will leave Egypt and return to their homeland (Krinsky).

### Verse 14

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:14:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:14:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:14:1)


**וימררו.** ידוע הוא כי התי"ו סימן לנקבות על הרוב, והמ"ם סימן לזכרים, כמו מועדות (דה"ב ח יג) ומועדים (ברא' א יד), ודרך חכמי ספרד כי בניני הפעלים שמורים ולא תחסר אות מן השרש, ואינם כן, רק שמות דברים יאמרו כאשר נמצאו, כי יחיד מן מועדות מועד לא מועדה, כאשר יאמר החכם בעיניו כי מן מקום יאמר מקומים וממקומות מקומה אולי יפקח עיניו ויראה, כי מן בכור יאמר בכורים, למכה מצרים בבכוריהם (תה' קלו י), והנה ובכורות בקרך (דבר' יד כג), א"כ יהיה היחיד בכורה, וככה לבנים, לא יאמר לבן כ"א לבנה:


AND THEY MADE THEIR LIVES BITTER. It is known that the *tav*, in a majority of instances, is the sign of the feminine plural and the *mem* of the masculine plural. Compare, *mo’adot* (seasons) (II Chron. 8:13) and *mo’adim* (seasons) (Gen. 1:14).¹²⁴ is feminine. *Mo’adim* is masculine. According to the Spanish scholars verbal forms are kept and do not drop any of their root letters.¹²⁵ However, this is not the case with nouns. Nouns are only employed as found in Scripture,¹²⁶ for the singular of *mo’adot* (seasons) is *mo’ed*, not *mo’adah* as the person who thinks he is so brilliant believes.¹²⁷ is a feminine plural form. *Mo’ed* is a masculine singular form. These two forms are inconsistent. The unnamed sage thus postulated that a female form *mo’adah* existed, the plural of which is *mo’adot*. However, no such form is found in Scripture. The latter would maintain that the plural of *makom* (place)¹²⁸ is masculine. is *mekomim*¹²⁹ is *mekomot. Mekomot* has a feminine ending. and the singular of *mekomot* (places) is *mekomah*.¹³⁰ is a feminine form. We thus see that the plural and singular forms of nouns are not consistent. Perhaps he will open his eyes and see that the plural of *bekhor* (first-born) is *bekhorim*, as in *To Him that smote Egypt in their first-born* (bekhorehem) (Ps. 136:10).¹³¹ (their first-born) is the word *bekhorim* with the pronominal suffix. However, we also encounter the form *bekhorot* (firstlings) in *and the firstlings of thy herd* (Deut. 14:23). Now, shall the singular of *bekhorot* be *bekhorah*?¹³². Thus we see once again that the singular (*bekhor*) and the plural (*bekhorot*) are based on different forms of the noun. The same is the case with *levenim* (bricks).¹³³ is feminine even though it has a masculine ending. Its singular is *levenah*,¹³⁴ is feminine. not *leven*.¹³⁵

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:14:3

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:14:3](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:14:3)


**אשר עבדו בהם.** ישרתו בעבור שנים, עבדו בהם בפרך, וגזרת עבד בלא בי"ת אחריה היא עבודת העבד וככה "עבדתיך" (ברא' ל כו), ואם אחריה בי"ת הוא על ב' דברים, האחד בעבור, כמו "ויעבד ישראל באשה" (הושע יב יג) והשני לא תעבוד בו בפרך כדרך "אשר לא עובד בה" (דברי' כא ג), וככה אשר לא יעבד בו (שם שם ד), כי כתוב והארץ הנשמה תעבד (יחז' לו לד) ועל הדרך הזה "כנושה כאשר נושה בו" (ישעי' כד ב):


WHEREIN THEY MADE THEM SERVE. The word *avedu* (they made them serve) is to be read as if written twice. Our verse is to be read as if it were written: wherein they made them serve, they made them serve with rigor. When a verb from the root *ayin, bet, dalet* is not followed by a *bet* it refers to work performed by a slave. This is the meaning of *avadatikha* (I have served thee) (Gen. 30:26).¹³⁷ However, when the verb is followed by a *bet* it has one of the following two meanings. It means for the sake of, as in *va-ya’avod yisrael be-ishah* (and Israel served for a wife) (Hos. 12:13).¹³⁸ following *va-ya’avod* has the meaning of: for the sake of. Thus *be-ishah* means: for the sake of a woman. Its other meaning is illustrated by *thou shalt not make him to serve* (lo ta’avod bo) *with rigor*,¹³⁹. The words *with rigor* come from Lev. 25:43. I.E.’s point is that in this case the *bet* (bo) has the meaning of with him. which is like *which hath not been wrought with* (lo ubbad bah) (Deut. 21:3).¹⁴⁰ is the indirect object, for the meaning of *lo ubbad bah* is: *which hath not been wrought with* (Weiser). *Which may neither be plowed* (lo ye’aved bo) (Deut. 21:4)¹⁴¹ is the indirect object, for the verse literally reads: which may neither be plowed in, i.e., land that no one worked with. is similar, for we find, *And the land that was desolate shall be tilled* (Ezek. 36:34).¹⁴², the indirect object. Hence when the *bet* is there it represents the indirect object (Filwarg). In a like manner Scripture reads, *As with the lender, so with the borrower* (nosheh vo) (Is. 24:2).¹⁴³ (bo) is the *bet* of the indirect object and means with him (Weiser).

### Verse 16

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:16:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:16:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:16:1)


**ויאמר בילדכן את העבריות.** כל שהוא ממשפחת עבר יקרא עברי, ועל אמונתו יקרא עברי על כן אבי כל בני עבר (ברא' י כא) הבא מעבר הנהר, עבר הנהר משתי העברים:


WHEN YE DO THE OFFICE OF A MIDWIFE TO THE HEBREW WOMEN. Whoever comes from the family of *ever* (Eber)¹⁴⁶) was the ancestor of Abraham (Gen. 11:14-29). Hence his descendants are known as *ivrim* (Hebrews). is called a Hebrew. One is called a Hebrew because of his faith.¹⁴⁷, is also called a Hebrew (Filwarg). Krinsky explains: One is called a Hebrew both by virtue of descent from *ever* and also because of his or her belief in the faith of Abraham. Hence descendants of *ever* who do not believe in the faith of Abraham are not called Hebrews. Hence *the children of Eber* (Ever) in *the father of all the children of Eber* (Gen. 10:21) refers to those who came from the side (*ever*) of the river.¹⁴⁸. The reference is to the eastern side of the Euphrates. The side of the river refers to one of the banks of the river.¹⁴⁹ in Hebrew can refer to a person or to the side of a river. Gen. 10:21 reads, *And unto Shem, the father of all the children of Eber* (ever)…*also were born children*. Now Shem lived before Eber was born. I.E. assumed that Scripture would not report someone as being the ancestor of a person not yet born. Hence Eber in this verse cannot refer to a person. It refers to those born on one of the sides of the Euphrates. This interpretation contradicts the one I.E. gives in Genesis and elsewhere in Exodus. Cf. Gen. 10:21 and Ex. 21:2. Krinsky suggests emending “hence” to “or.” In other words, I.E. offers an alternative interpretation to the one he gave in Genesis and will offer later on in Exodus. Filwarg, on the other hand, suggests emending the text to read: Hence they err who say that *the children of Eber*, in *the father of all the children of Eber*, refers to those who came from the side of the river. For the side of the river refers to one of the sides of the river. In other words, *ever* cannot refer only to the western bank of the river where Abraham came from. A river has two sides and *ever* might refer to the eastern bank of the river, which is not the place that the Hebrews originally came from.

[THEN SHE SHALL LIVE.] The word *va-chayah* (then she shall live) is irregular and presents a very difficult grammatical problem. The rules of grammar require *va-chayetah*¹⁵⁵ is masculine. *Va-chayetah* is feminine. Since the Bible speaks of *a daughter* the latter form should have been used. because the *heh* of the root¹⁵⁶. changes to a *tav*,¹⁵⁷ as it does in the construct in the case of the word *chayat* (beast of)¹⁵⁸. in *and to every beast of the earth* (Gen. 1:30). The reason for the change is that the *heh* and the *tav* are similar in appearance when written. The only difference between them is the extension of the dot that is within the *heh*. For the letter *tav* is first a *heh*. It is only when the dot is extended that it becomes a *tav*.¹⁵⁹ is open on the left side with the exception of a tiny line (referred to as a dot by I.E.) at the bottom. The *tav* is closed on both the right and left sides. Thus by drawing from the small line (the dot) to the top of the letter, the *heh* becomes a *tav*. However, the *tav* and the *heh* are pronounced completely differently.¹⁶⁰ They also have different names.¹⁶¹, one will not think he heard *tav*. This proves that our form of the letters is the original Hebrew script.¹⁶² 22a) over whether the original script of the Torah was identical to the script currently in use (the so-called Assyrian script), or whether the Torah was originally written in a script known as “Hebrew script.” In the Assyrian script the *heh* and the *tav* resemble each other. In the “Hebrew script” they are totally different. The fact that the Torah substitutes a *heh* for a *tav* because they resemble each other shows that the Torah was originally written in the Assyrian script. Historically speaking, the opinion that the Torah was given in “Hebrew script” is right, for all Hebrew writing extant from the period of the first commonwealth is in the “Hebrew script.”Generally speaking, the root of the word *chai* (lived) and the root of the word *chayyim* (life) are in doubt, for the grammarians have concluded that the root of the word *chai* (lived) in *And Arpachshad lived* (Gen. 11:12) is *chet, yod, yod*. The word *tam* (spent) in *how that our money is all spent* (Gen. 47:18) is similar, for it comes from the root *tav, mem, mem*.¹⁶³ The grammarians also agree that the plural of the root *chet, yod, yod* is *chayyim* (life). However, in my opinion we are dealing with an irregular root.¹⁶⁴ forms, the word *chai* is written as if it came from the root *chet, yod, yod*. On the other hand, it is conjugated in the other *kal* forms as if it came from the root *chet, yod, heh*. If this is not so¹⁶⁵ let someone show me a case where this root is conjugated in the imperfect according to the paradigm of *chet, gimel, gimel*, namely, *achog* (I will celebrate), *tachog* (you will celebrate), *yachog* (he will celebrate), *la-chog* (to celebrate).¹⁶⁶ imperfect. If the root of *chai* were *chet, yod, yod*, it should be conjugated *achoy, yachoy, la-choy* in the imperfect or like *sov* (go about) or *sobu* (walk about) in *Walk about Zion* (Ps. 48:13) and *sobbi* (go about)¹⁶⁷ or *sobbi* is *samekh, bet, bet. Sov* and *sobbi* are imperative forms. in *Go about the city* (Is. 23:16). This is proof that the word *chai* comes from a root ending in a *heh*. The fact that we do not find the root of *chai* conjugated in any of the above-mentioned forms is proof that it belongs to those verbs whose stems end in a *heh*,¹⁶⁸. I.E. is usually not this verbose and repetitious. Filwarg suggests that from “the fact” until “for we say” is an explanatory gloss that was incorporated into the text. The original reading was: This is proof that the word *chai* comes from a root ending in a *heh.*, for we say *echyeh, nichyeh*, etc. for we say *echeyeh* (I will live), *nichyeh* (we will live), *eheyeh* (I will be), *tiheyeh* (you will be), *yiheyeh* (he will be), all of which come from the root *heh, yod, heh*. Now if this is the case it comes from the root *chet, yod, heh* and is like the word *haya* (was).¹⁶⁹. The fact that we find the word *chai* (lived) employed as a third person perfect in *arpachshad chai* (Arpachshad lived) (Gen. 11:12) does not disturb us.¹⁷⁰. We are not bothered by the aforementioned even though it appears that *chai* comes from a double root.¹⁷¹ is the normal conjugation of the word if it comes from the root *chet, yod, yod*. I.E. is not disturbed by this because he believes this root to be irregular. See note 155. What forced me to come to this conclusion is the fact that I saw that there is no root in Hebrew that ends in a *vav*.¹⁷². See further in I.E.’s note. The word *shalev* (at ease) (Job 16:12) does not disprove my contention.¹⁷³ appears to come from the root *shin, lamed, vav*. Its *vav* is in place of a *heh*,¹⁷⁴. since the letters *alef, heh, vav, yod* interchange. Proof that what I say is correct is the word *shalu* (secure) in *Wherefore are all they secure that deal treacherously* (Job 12:1). For the root of *shalu* is *shin, lamed, heh*.¹⁷⁵ is the noun form of the verb *shalu*. Hence the root of *shalev* must be the same as the root of *shalu*.I will now explain to you why a *vav* is never employed as a third letter of a root. The latter is so because the *vav* serves as a third person singular suffix, as in the words *avdo va-amato* (his man-servant nor his maid-servant) (Ex. 20:14). The *vav* also serves as the sign of the plural, as in *peru u-revu* (be fruitful and multiply) (Gen. 1:22). There are also superfluous *vavs*, as in *beno be’or* (the son of Beor) (Num. 24:3).¹⁷⁶. Hence the *vav* of *beno* is superfluous. Now if the *vav* was also used as the final letter of a root it would be confused with one of the three types of *vavs* that we have just mentioned, namely, the *vav* indicating a third person singular suffix, the *vav* indicating a plural, and the superfluous *vav*; we could not then ascertain the meaning of the word.¹⁷⁷ is a root letter or a suffix (Krinsky). The same is also true of the *yod*. The *yod* cannot serve as the final letter of a stem because it is used as a first person singular suffix, as in the word *yadi* (my hand) (Gen. 42:37). It is also employed as a first person plural suffix, as in the word *yadai* (my hands) (Deut. 9:15). It is also the sign of the plural construct, as in *yede* (the hands of) in *The hands of women full of compassion* (Lamentations 4:10). It is used as the sign of the feminine imperative, as in *de’i and re’i* (know and consider) (I Sam. 25:17). It is used to indicate relationship, as in *ha-ivri o ha-ivriyah* (a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman) (Deut. 15:22). The *yod* is also used superfluously in verbs, as in *ha-magbihi* (that is enthroned) (Ps. 113:5) and in *le-hoshivi* (that He may set him) (Ps. 113:8).¹⁷⁸ and *le-hoshiv*. Hence the *yods* are superfluous. It is used superfluously with nouns, as in *beni atono* (his ass’s colt) (Gen. 49:11)¹⁷⁹. Hence the *yod* is superfluous. and also with particles, as in *zulati* (save) (Deut. 1:36) and *minni ephrayim* (out of Ephraim) (Judges 5:14).¹⁸⁰ and *min*. Hence the *yods* are superfluous. For these reasons the *yod* is not employed as a final root letter lest it be confused with one of the above-noted *yods*. Therefore I maintain that the word *va-chayah* (then shall she live) is irregular and is a variant of *va-chayetah*. It belongs, as I have already explained, in the family of verbs ending in a *heh*.

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 1:18:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:18:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/1:18:1)


**ויקרא.** הנכון בנות מות כי הפכתן מצותי, ואין הפרש בין ותאמרנה עבר, כמו ותאכלנה הפרות (ברא' מא ד) ובין כשידבר עליהן לנכח עצמן, בהכנס הוי"ו הפתוח וככה מדוע עשיתן ותחיין:


AND THE KING OF EGYPT CALLED FOR THE MIDWIVES, AND SAID UNTO THEM. You deserve to die¹⁸³ to *hinkhen*. because you have not obeyed my command.¹⁸⁴, etc. What he meant was, why have you violated my command and thereby incurred the death penalty. There is no difference in the form of the word *va-tomarnah* (said) in which the *vav* is vocalized with a *pattach* when it is in the third person perfect, like the word *va-tokhalnah* (did eat) in *And the ill-favoured, and lean-fleshed kine did eat* (Gen. 41:4), and when it is used as a second person perfect.¹⁸⁵ to the corresponding imperfect form. Thus *va-tomarnah* may mean either “and they said” or “and you (plural) said,” for *tomarnah* means either “they will say” or “you (plural) will say.” However, they differ in the regular perfect, for the normal second person form is *amarten* and the regular third person form is *ameru*. The same, of course, applies to the word *va-techayyenah* (and have saved). Indeed, I.E.’s comments are directed to explain this word, for *va-techayyenah* in our verse means “and ye have saved” while in verse 17 it means “and they saved.” Hence I.E.’s paraphrase: “why have ye done this thing and saved.” The meaning of our verse is: Why have ye done this thing and preserved the man-children alive?

AND GOD DEALT WELL. When a root begins with a *yod*, the *yod* does not always drop out when the verb is conjugated,¹⁸⁶. The word *va-yetev* (dealt well) is an example. At other times a *vav* is substituted for the *yod*, as in *va-yoshev* (He maketh to dwell) in *And there He maketh the hungry to dwell* (Ps. 107:36). The root of *va-yoshev* is *yod, shin, bet*, as the root of *va-yetev* is *yod, tet, bet*.¹⁸⁷ of a root beginning with a *yod* changes to a *vav* when the word is conjugated in the *hifil*. However, *va-yetev*, which comes from the root *yod, tet, bet* and is a *hifil* form retains its *yod*. Hence I.E.’s comment.*And God dealt well* is explained by what follows next, i.e., *He* (God) *made them houses*. The meaning of *He made them houses* is similar to *that the Lord make thee a house* (II Sam. 7:11).¹⁸⁸

Note that the verb *yare’u* (feared) is neither transitive nor intransitive, because its meaning is, to be afraid of someone.¹⁸⁹ means to be afraid of someone. The one who is frightened does nothing to the source of his fright. Hence the verb is not transitive. On the other hand, the frightened person does nothing to himself; i.e., he does not scare himself. Hence the verb is not intransitive (Weiser). Hence the correct way of saying “feared the Lord” would be *yare’u me’et Adonai*.¹⁹⁰ connects a transitive verb with the direct object. However, *yare*, as I.E. has noted, is not transitive. Hence I.E. notes that *et* is short for *me’et.*, the literal meaning of our text being: were afraid of God. Obadiah used a short form when he said, *yare et Adonai* (fear the Lord) (I Kings 18:12).¹⁹¹ is short for *me’et*. It is for this reason that the word *nora* (revered)¹⁹² is the passive form of the *kal*. Since the verb *yare* is not transitive it does not have a *nifal* counterpart. The word *nora* (revered) is thus not a *nifal* verb even though it has the form of a *nifal*. does not come in the *nifal* form as the words *nolad* (was born) (I Chron. 2:3), *nishbar* (broken) (Ps. 51:19), and *ve-nidkeh* (and contrite) (*Ibid.*) do.¹⁹³ verbs. The intelligent will understand why.¹⁹⁴ is not *a nifal* verb even though it comes in that form (Krinsky). However, I.E. uses this formula when he hints at some secret meaning. He apparently does so here. However, it is hard to ascertain what he is hinting at.

AND THE WOMAN CONCEIVED. There is no doubt that Aaron was older than Moses.⁸ 38. The printed manuscripts read, “There is no doubt that what we noted (*kemo she-hizkarnu*) is correct. For Aaron was older than Moses.” This sentence is obviously difficult to unravel, for what bearing does the fact that Aaron was older than Moses have upon Amram marrying his aunt? Krinsky and Netter attempt to explain it and in my opinion fail to do so. The reading of the Vatican manuscript appears to be correct, and the words *kemo she-hizkarnu* are most likely a gloss by a scribe who thought that “there is no doubt” refers to what I.E. said earlier namely, that Amram married his aunt. Our sages similarly received a tradition that Puah⁹ and Miriam are one and the same person.¹⁰ 11b. It is also written, *And his sister stood afar off* (v. 4).¹¹Now we know that the four hundred-year period¹² which ended in Israel’s redemption started with the day that Isaac was born, for Isaac alone is considered to be Abraham’s seed.¹³ Now Isaac was sixty years old when he begot Jacob,¹⁴ and Jacob was eighty-five years old when he begot Reuben,¹⁵ and one hundred and thirty years old when he descended into Egypt.¹⁶ If we add the sixty years of Isaac to the one hundred and thirty of Jacob we come up with a hundred and ninety years. We are thus left with two hundred and ten years.¹⁷ We then subtract the seventy years that Joseph lived afterwards¹⁸ and we are left with one hundred and forty years. Now Levi was forty-three years old when he came down to Egypt¹⁹ and he outlived Joseph by twenty-two years.²⁰ Thus one hundred and eighteen years are left. For the verse states, *So Joseph died, being a hundred and ten years old* (Gen. 50:26).²¹ Now when did the new king reign? For how many years did the Israelites build the store-cities? Behold close to the birth of Moses it was decreed that all male children be put to death.²²Ben Zuta²³ says whoever relates a story will not out of respect mention the most honored first.²⁴ Therefore when Scripture states, *and she* (Jochebed) *bore unto Amram Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister* (Num. 26:59), it indicates that Miriam was the youngest.²⁵ Now the “blind one” (Ben Zuta) forgot Shem, Ham, and Japheth, concerning whom it is written, *and Noah begot Shem, Ham and Japheth* (Gen. 5:32). Now Japheth was the eldest of the three.²⁶ Furthermore, Scripture states, *There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife* (Gen. 49:31) even though Sarah was buried in the cave of Machpelah thirty-eight years²⁷ before Abraham was interred there. Note that the *nun* is often dropped or is swallowed by a *dagesh* when it is the first root letter of a verb, as in the case of the *nun* of *gesh*²⁸. in *gesh holah* (stand back) (Gen. 19:9) and *va-yiggash* (came near)²⁹. The *dagesh* in the *gimel* compensates for the missing *nun*. in *Then Judah came near unto him* (Gen. 44:18). The *nun* is also dropped when it serves as the middle letter of a root,³⁰ as in the case of *af* (anger)³¹. in *And anger also went up against Israel* (Ps. 78:21). Observe, the middle *nun* is swallowed. Therefore the *peh* of *appo* (his wrath) in *that his wrath was kindled* (Gen. 39:19) and the *peh* of *appekah* (thine anger) in *Thine anger is turned away* (Is. 12:1) receive a *dagesh*. The same is true of the *nun* of the root *nun, tav, nun* in the word *titti* (that I give) (Gen. 29:19), for *titti* is like *tinti*³². If the final *nun* was not dropped, *titti* would have been written *tinti*. because its final *tav*³³ comes from the root *nun, tav, nun*. It does not come from a root ending in a *tav*, for its last *tav* is a first person suffix. is not a root letter. It is rather like the *tavs* of *shivti* (my downsitting) (Ps. 139:2), *lekhti* (when I went) (I Kings 2:8), and *lidti* (I delivered) (I Kings 3:18).³⁴ is a first person suffix. It is also so at the end of the word,³⁵ of the root *nun, tav, nun* at times drop out but its final *nun* is also omitted at times. as in *tet* (to put) in *to put the dread of thee* (Deut. 2:25) and in *titti* (that I give) in *that I give her to thee* (Gen. 29:19). The same is true of nouns. The word for daughter (*bat*) should have been *banah* since the feminine of *ben* (son) is *banah*. However, in this case it would have been confused with the verb *banah* (hath built), as in *that hath built* (banah) *a new house* (Deut. 20:5). A *tav* was therefore substituted for the *heh*.³⁶, not *banah*. I.E. will soon explain why the *nun* was dropped from *banat*, the Hebrew word for daughter being *bat*. It is similar to *givirah* (lady) and *geveret* (lady) as well as to *atarah* (crown) and *ateret* (crown) in which we find both the construct and the absolute forms used in the absolute.³⁷ is usually in the absolute. However, its form is that of a word in the construct. We find the same thing with the word *geveret. Givirah* is in the absolute; *geveret* is in the construct. Nevertheless, the construct form is used in the absolute. Similarly *atarah* and *ateret*. So too, *bat* means both daughter and daughter of. Compare, *ateret* (crown of) in *A crown of glory* (Prov. 4:7). It should be noted that the *nun* was also dropped for the sake of easing the pronunciation of the word.³⁸ of *banah* changed to a *tav*, but its *nun* was dropped. Thus *banah* became *bat*. Hence the word is enunciated *bat* (daughter). The word *bitto* (his daughter) in *Rachel his daughter* (Gen. 29:6) is similar to the word *amitto* (his truth) which is the word *emet* (truth) with the third person pronominal suffix.³⁹ comes from the root *bet, nun, heh. Emet* comes from the root *alef, mem, nun*. In the words *emet* and *amitto* the *nun* is missing. Hence *bitto* is like *amitto*. Compare, *chasdo va-amitto* (His mercy and His truth) (Gen. 24:27). Thus the *tav* is the sign of the feminine and the *nun* is swallowed up.⁴⁰ of *bat* takes the place of the *heh* of *banah*. Additionally, the *nun* is dropped, hence the word *bat*. The plural of truth is *emunot*, and not *amitot* or *amitiyot*.⁴¹ is *alef, mem, nun*. Similarly, the plural of daughters is *banot*, not *batot* or *battim*.⁴². The plural of *banah* is *banot*, whereas the plural of *bat* is *batot* or *battim*. I.E.’s intention here was to explain the form *bat* in verse 1.

THREE MONTHS. Some say that Moses was born in the seventh month following his conception.⁵⁰ However, this interpretation like so many others is Midrashic,⁵¹ for the Egyptians had no way of determining when the woman⁵² conceived. In my opinion Scripture relates the months that she was able to hide the child⁵³ since it is impossible for anyone to predict when a women will give birth.⁵⁴ It is also far-fetched to say that Moses was born in the seventh month following conception because those so born are undersized.⁵⁵ Those born in the eleventh month are healthier and live longer, as most children are born close to the ninth month.⁵⁶ One who knows the time of conception is able to ascertain the time of birth, and one who knows the time of birth can ascertain the time of conception. This was established by the ancients. I myself have tried it five times.⁵⁷ For the degree and place of the moon and its constellation at the moment of conception is also the degree of the constellation that flowers at the moment of begetting The degree which flowers at the moment of impregnation will also be the degree at which the moon will be found at the time of birth.⁵⁸ Now the time set aside⁵⁹, (the time set aside). However, since I.E. gives three time periods, what he must mean is the minimum time. Filwarg suggests reading *ha-katan* (the minimum) in place of *ha-kotzev*. for carrying a child is two hundred and fifty nine and a third days.⁶⁰ The median time for pregnancy is two hundred and seventy-three days.⁶¹ The maximum time for being with child is two hundred and eighty-seven days.⁶² Those learned in astrology will admit this.⁶³ rather than *yodu*. The birth of the tribes⁶⁴ does not refute this,⁶⁵ because the order of their listing is no proof that they were born prematurely.⁶⁶ We find many such instances in the Torah.⁶⁷ It is therefore possible that Rachel gave her handmaid to Jacob when Simeon was born, that Issachar was born before Asher,⁶⁸ and that Dinah was Zebulun’s twin.⁶⁹ (Gen. 30:21). *Prima facie*, it appears that Dinah was born some time after the birth of Zebulun. I.E. argues that this is not so. He suggests that *afterwards* means a few moments later, as it does in Gen. 30:21. Hence the phrase *and afterwards* in *and afterwards she bore a daughter* (Gen. 30:21) is similar to *And after that came forth his brother* (Gen. 25:26). For *and she conceived* is not mentioned for each one. Also, *And it came to pass, when the seasons were come about* (I Sam. 1:20) refers to three seasons.⁷⁰ (tekufat) *of days came to pass, and Hannah conceived and bore a son* (I Sam. 20). Mar Zutra explains that *tekufot* (seasons) refers to six months (a *tekufah*, a season is three months) and days, to two days. Cf. *Rosh Ha-Shanah* 11a. I.E. disagrees. According to him, *seasons* refers to three seasons (nine months). Hence Samuel was not born prematurely.

ונדגש צדי"ק הצּפינו כדגשות קו"ף אם יִקְּרֵךְ עון (ש"א כח י) לדבר בם צחות ובעבור היות הצדי"ק בשו"א נע, נרפה הפ"א שהיה ראוי להדגש, והוא שם הפועל מהבנין הכבד הנוסף, ואין צורך לבקש למה לא צפנתהו עוד, אולי השכנות המצריות שמעו קולו כי לא היו לבדם דרים בארץ רעמסס, וכתב ושאלה אשה משכנתה (למטה ג כב):


[HIDE HIM.] The *tzadi* of *hatzefino* (hide him), like the *kof* in the word *yikkrekh* (happen to thee) in *there shall no punishment happen to thee* (I Sam. 28:10), receives a *dagesh* so that these words may be clearly pronounced.⁷¹ in it is emphasized; i.e., the word is sounded *hatzefino* (*dagesh* in *tzadi*) rather than *hatzpino* (no *dagesh* in the *tzadi*). I.E. makes this point because there is no grammatical reason for a *dagesh* to be placed in *hatzefino* or *yikkrekh*. The *peh* in *hatzefino* should have received a *dagesh*. However, it does not because the *tzadi* is vocalized with a mobile *sheva. Hatzefino* is a *hifil* infinitive. There is no reason to speculate as to why Jochebed did not hide him for a longer period of time.⁷² Perhaps the Egyptian neighbors heard his voice,⁷³ for the Hebrews were not the only inhabitants of the land of Rameses.⁷⁴ For it is written, *but every women shall ask of her neighbor* (Ex. 3:22).⁷⁵

[AN ARK OF BULRUSHES.] The words *tevat gome* (an ark of bulrushes) are penultimately accented because the cantillical note is placed on the first syllable of the word *gome* (bulrushes).⁷⁶ is penultimately accented; so is *tevat*. I.E. explains that when two words are connected by cantillical notes and the second word is penultimately accented, so is the first word. This is so even though the word is ordinarily ultimately accented.

AND DAUBED IT. The *heh of va-tachmerah* (and daubed it) is silent. It is like the *heh* of the word *lah* (it) in *and called it* (lah) *Nobah, after his own name* (Num. 32:42).⁷⁷ which serves as a pronominal suffix is vocalized with a *mappik* and is thus sounded. However, this is not the case with the pronominal *heh* in *va-tachmerah*. I.E. thus points out that the *mappik* is occasionally omitted from the *heh* which serves as a pronominal suffix. The word *va-tachmerah* (and daubed it) is derived from the word *ba-chemar* (with slime).⁷⁸ is a denominative of *chemar*. *Chemar* (slime) is a red sticky clay which is found in the Land of Israel. The word *chemar* (slime) in *full of slime pits* (Gen. 14:10) is similar. This substance is called *al chamara* in Arabic. Jochebed did this⁷⁹ for she said, “Let me not look upon the death of the child.”⁸⁰ Perhaps the sister⁸¹ of Moses prophesied that she do this.⁸² God’s thoughts are very deep. Who can know His secrets? By Him alone are actions weighed.⁸³ Perhaps God arranged things so that Moses would grow up in a royal house and his spirit would thereby be exalted through learning and practice.⁸⁴ He would thus not possess a base spirit habituated to being in the house of slaves. Do you not see that Moses killed an Egyptian because the latter committed an act of violence⁸⁵ and that he saved the daughters of Midian from the shepherds because they were acting violently in trying to water their flocks with the water which the women had drawn?⁸⁶ One more thing: had Moses grown up among his brothers and had they known him from his youth they would not have feared him because they would have considered him as one of themselves.⁸⁷

AND HIS SISTER STOOD AFAR OFF. The word *va-tetatzav* (stood) is irregular because a missing silent letter⁸⁸ of *va-tetatzav* is vocalized with a *tzere*. The *tzere* is sounded as if a *yod*, a silent letter, followed it, hence the phrase a “missing silent letter” for the *tzere*. has been substituted for a *yod*⁸⁹ is *yod, tzadi, bet*, and that its *tav* prefix is vocalized with a *tzere* rather than with a *chirik* to compensate for the missing *yod*. between the two *tavs*.Rabbi Moses Ha-Kohen⁹⁰ says that a *tav* is suffixed to the words *laredet* (to descend) and *la-geshet* (to approach) because the first root letter of these words is missing.⁹¹ is *yod, resh, dalet*. The stem of *la-geshet* is *nun, gimel, shin*. The *yod* is dropped in the infinitive and according to Rabbi Moses is compensated for by the *tav*. That is also the case with the word *la-da’at* (to know).⁹². This word is vocalized with a *pattach* because the *ayin* is a guttural.⁹³ and not *la-de’et*. I.E. makes this point because he wants to show that *la-da’at* and *la-geshet* belong to the same form even though they are vocalized differently. Now in the word *le-de’ah* (to know)⁹⁴, and is an infinitive. *Prima facie*, it should have been written *la-da’at*. the *tav* was changed to a *heh*,⁹⁵ is a variant of *la-da’at*, and what I.E. said about the latter applies to the former as well. as in the case of the word *tenah* (rehearsed)⁹⁶ is *nun, tav, nun*. The infinitive form is *tet* (or *te-nat*). In *te-nah* a *heh* has been substituted for the *tav*. Hence *le-de’ah* and *la-da’at* are similar to *tet* (*te-nat*) and *te-nah*. in *Whose majesty is rehearsed above the heavens* (Ps. 8:2).

TO BATHE IN THE RIVER. As was the custom of Egyptian women. Scripture notes that her maidens walked by the riverside — the meaning of *yad* (side, place) here is the same as that of *yad* (place) in *Thou shalt have a place* (Deut. 23:13)⁹⁷ means a hand. For a princess would not go among the flags, and the ark was placed far from the shore so that no one passing by would touch it. Furthermore, from a grammatical point of view the word *amah* (handmaid) cannot mean an arm, because its *mem* does not have a *dagesh* while the *mem* of *ammah* (cubit) in *A cubit shall be the length thereof* (Gen. 30:2) does.⁹⁹ (cubit) means an arm. Additionally, *ammah* (cubit) in *A cubit shall be the length thereof* refers to a measure and not to an arm.¹⁰⁰ with *ammah, ammah* does not mean her arm. It means her cubit.

AND PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER SAID TO HER: GO. *Lekhi* (go) is like *shevi* (sit).¹¹² is vocalized with a *tzere* beneath the *lamed*. The usual way of vocalizing this form (the imperative) is with a *sheva*. I.E. points out that this is also the case with the word *shevi*. It is usually vocalized with a *sheva*. However, in Jer. 29:5 we find its plural form vocalized with a *tzere*. The reason for the change from *sheva* to *tzere* is that these words come at the end of a verse. These words are the imperative forms of *va-yelekh* (and he went) and *va-yeshev* (and he dwelt).

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 2:9:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/2:9:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/2:9:1)


**היליכי.** כמו היניקי כי שנים שרשים הם, ילך, גם הלך, והטעם אחד, כי אין הה"א מאותיות המשך על כן ה"א אחרת כמוה ועוד כי האל"ף גם היו"ד הוי"ו ימצאו בתוך המלה, פעם נכתבים, ופעם נחים נמצאים במבטא לא במכתב, ופעם נעדרים והה"א לעולם באמצע היא נראית ומלת בלטיהם (למטה ז כב) איננה כמו בלהטיהם (שם שם יא) כאשר אפרש:


TAKE. *Helikhi* (take) is like *heniki* (nurse)¹¹³ (and nurse it) is a combination of *ve-heniki* (and nurse) and *oto* (it). I.E. points out that both *helikhi* and *heniki* are one and the same form, that is, *peh, yod, hifil* imperatives. because the roots *yod, lamed, kaf* and *heh, lamed, kaf* are two roots with one meaning.¹¹⁴ (take) literally means go. I.E. maintains that there are two roots in Hebrew for the word go, *heh, lamed, kaf*, as in the word *halakhti*, and *yod*, *lamed, kaf*, as in the word *va-yelekh*. I.E. believes that the root of *helikhi* is *yod, lamed, kaf*, the *heh* being the *heh* of the *hifil* conjugation. See note 112. For the *heh* is not one of the implied vowel letters.¹¹⁵, and *yod* are implied in the vowels *kamatz, cholam*, and *tzere*; i.e., the words vocalized with these vowels are sounded as if followed by an *alef, vav*, or *yod*. Now when a letter is implied in a vowel it is occasionally omitted. If the *heh* was an implied letter then it is possible that the root of *helikhi* is *heh, lamed, kaf* with the *heh* implied. For the *heh* of *helikhi* is not a root letter. It is rather the *heh* of the *hifil* imperative. Therefore the other *heh* is also like it.¹¹⁶ of the root (the other *heh*) should have appeared in the word *helikhi;* i.e., if *helikhi* came from the root *heh, lamed, kaf* the word should have been spelled *hehlikhi*. Furthermore, the *alef* and likewise the *yod* and the *vav* are found in the middle of a word at times written and at times silent, that is, pronounced but unwritten,¹¹⁷ but the *heh* is always visible when in the middle of a word. The words *be-latehem* (with their secret arts) (Ex. 7:22) and *be-lahatehem* (with their secret arts) (Ex. 7:11) are not, as I will explain,¹¹⁸ one and the same word.¹¹⁹, the second one with a *heh. Prima facie*, they are the same word with the missing *heh* implied. I.E. says no. He believes them to be two distinctive words with roots of their own.

ותאמר. אמר הגאון כי היליכי הם שתי מלות ולא דבר נכונה, רק היא מלה אחת על משקל והיניקהו לי, כמו שאמרתי, והוא מהבנין הכבד הנוסף, גם אמר שהוא כמו "הא לך", והנה הא, כמו וגם אני הא (יחז' טז מג), ואנחנו לא מצאנו בכל המקרא לנקבה ליכי כ"א לך רק היא מלה אחת:


AND PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER SAID. Saadiah Gaon says that *helikhi* (take) is a composite of two words.¹²⁰ imperative from the root *yod, lamed, kaf* but rather a composite of the words *he* and *lekhi*. However, the Gaon spoke incorrectly. It is, as I have noted, one word following the paradigm of *ve-henikehu* (and nurse it) in *and nurse it for me*. The word is in the *hifil*. The Gaon also said that *helikhi* is a composite of the words *he* and *lakh*,¹²¹ means here is. Compare, *he lakhem zera* (lo, here is seed for you) (Gen. 47:2). *Lakh* (*lekhi* in the feminine) means to you. *He lekhi* thus means here is to you; i.e., take it. the meaning of *he* being the same as *he* (behold) in *Behold* (heh), *I will also bring thy way upon thy head* (Ezek. 16:43).¹²², etc. However, we do not find the form *lekhi* used in Scripture when a female is being addressed. The form employed by Scripture is *lakh*.¹²³ is a composite then it must be made up of the words *he* (here is) and *lekhi* (to you). However, the word for “to you” in the feminine is *lakh*, not *lekhi*. *Helikhi* (take) is thus one word.

ותניקהו. מעלומי העי"ן מן הפעלים השניים הנראים, והנה בפ' אחד שנים שרשים והטעם אחד, וככה היטיבי נגן (ישעי' כג טז) צווי, כמו הליכי, אך הטיבו כל אשר דברו (דבר' ה כד) כמו "והם הביאו אליו" (שמות לו ג) מעלומי העי"ן:

Hetivu* (they have well) comes from the root *tet, vav, bet*.

**וישמע.** ארץ מדין סרים היו אל משמעת פרעה, על כן הוצרך להיות רועה צאן שלא יעמוד בישוב אולי יכירוהו, וכאשר אמר לו השם שמת פרעה ועבדיו שברח מפניהם, ונולד לו בימים ההם בנו הקטן אז אמר ויצילני מחרב פרעה (למטה יח ד) כי כל ימי חייו היה ירא ממנו, ואחר שהזכיר וישב בארץ מדין שב לפרש למה ישב, כי בתחלה ישב לפני הבאר הידועה, כדרך "ויצא יעקב וגו' וילך" (ברא' כח י) ושב למר "ויפגע במקום" (שם פ' יא):


HEARD. The land of Midian was subservient to Pharaoh; hence Moses had to herd sheep and not live among people and be recognized.¹⁴⁰ It was at the time that his youngest son was born that God told Moses that Pharaoh and his servants from whom he had fled were dead. Upon hearing this Moses said, *and (God) delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh* (Ex. 18:4), as Moses feared Pharaoh as long as Pharaoh lived.¹⁴¹ (God) and *ezer* (help). Moses so named his son because, he said, *For the God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh* (Ex. 18:4). According to I.E., Moses gave this name to his son after learning that Pharaoh was dead and could no longer harm him. After noting *and (Moses) dwelt in the land of Midian*, Scripture goes back and explains why Moses dwelt in Midian.¹⁴² Moses first sat down before the specified well.¹⁴³. J.P.S. renders, *and he sat down by a well*. It is like *And Jacob went out from Beer-sheba and went to Haran* (Gen. 28:10). After stating the aforementioned the Pentateuch backsteps and states, *And he lighted upon the place*, etc. (Gen. 28:11).¹⁴⁴

### Verse 16

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 2:16:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/2:16:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/2:16:1)


**ולכהן.** הוא יתרו ולא רעואל וכל כהן שבמקרא משרת הוא לשם או לעכו"ם, והעד וכהנו לי (למטה כח מא) וכהני ד' (ישעי' סא ו) ויתרו היה כהן לשם כאשר אפרש עוד:


NOW THE PRIEST OF MIDIAN. The reference is to Jethro and not Reuel.¹⁴⁵ The term *kohen* (priest) in Scripture refers to one who ministers either to the Lord or before an idol. *That they may minister unto Me in the priest’s office* (Ex. 28:41)¹⁴⁶. If a *kohen* referred only to one who serves the Lord it would not be necessary to add the word *li* (unto me), as it would be understood that the reference is to priests of God. However, since one can also be a priest of idols the Bible adds the word *li*. The same is true with *the priest of the Lord*. If priests only referred to priests of the Lord there would be no reason for the Bible to add *of the Lord*. and *the priests of the Lord* (Is. 61:6) are proof of this. Jethro, as I will explain, was a priest of the Lord.¹⁴⁷

### Verse 17

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 2:17:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/2:17:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/2:17:1)


**ויבאו.** מ"ם ויגרשום כמו נו"ן שלא תתערב המלה עם הנו"ן הנוסף לעתיד, וככה צאנם במ"ם שלא להתחבר שני נונין:


AND THE SHEPHERDS CAME. The *mem* of *va-yegareshum* (and drove them away) has the same meaning as a *nun*.¹⁴⁸ in *and drove them away* refers to females, a *nun* should have been suffixed to *va-yegareshu* (and drove away) and the word read *va-yegareshun* rather than *va-yegareshum*. For the *mem* is a masculine suffix and the *nun* a feminine suffix. I.E. thus notes that although *va-yegareshum* is ordinarily masculine, here it is feminine. If *va-yegareshum* was spelled with a *nun*, the *nun* might be confused with a superfluous *nun*.¹⁴⁹ (or a superfluous *nun*) is added to the plural imperfect. Thus in place of the usual *yegareshu* (they will drive away) we have *yegareshun* (they will drive away). Now if our word was written *va-yegareshun* we would not know whether the word was merely plural with a superfluous *nun*, meaning: and they drove away, or if it was a plural with a feminine suffix, meaning: and they drove them away. To avoid this problem Scripture employed the masculine form here. Similarly, the word *tzonam* (their flock) is spelled with a *mem* so as not to combine two *nuns*.¹⁵⁰ is a feminine third person plural pronoun meaning their. Since our text speaks of flocks belonging to females we would expect to find *tzonan*, which has a feminine suffix, and not *tzonam*, which has a masculine suffix. I.E. explains that *tzonam* is used in place of *tzonan* because it is hard to pronounce two *nuns* in succession.

¹⁴⁹ At times an extra nun
¹⁵⁰ The nun

However, when Moses wrote the Torah about 40 years later, it was so known. Hence we see that Moses used contemporary terminology when he wrote the Torah. The place is called Horeb because of its great heat and lack of rainfall.², which means dry. As Moses noted,³ it is located three days’ journey from Egypt. There is no moisture there and the dryness is overpowering because the Nile is far away.

### Verse 2

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 3:2:1

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/3:2:1](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/3:2:1)


**וירא.** יש מפרשים בלבת אש בלהבת אש והנכון בעיני כי פירושו בלב האש כי כן מצאנו מה אמולה לבתך (יחז' טז), ור' אדנים אמר, אילו היה כן היה בלבת בחיר"ק תחת הלמ"ד, כמו אל גִנַת אגוז (שה"ש ו יא) והנה שכח וכְגַנָה זרועיה תצמיח (ישעי' סא יא):


APPEARED. Some interpret *be-labbat esh* to mean: in a flame of fire.⁴ (compare Num. 21:28). Those who say that *be-labbat* means in a flame explain that *be-labbat* is short for *be-lahavat*. However, it appears to me that its meaning is, in the heart⁵ in the word *labbat*. of the fire, for we indeed find, *How weak is thy heart* (libbatekh) (Ezek. 16:30).⁶ is the word *libbah* (heart) plus the second person pronominal suffix. Thus *libbah* means heart and *labbat* means heart of. It should be noted that the more familiar form for heart is *lev*. However, Rabbi Adonim⁷ says that if this were so, then *be-labbat* would have been vocalized with a *chirik* beneath the *lamed* like the word *ginnat* (garden of) in *I went down into the garden of nuts* (Canticles 6:11).⁸ is the construct form of *libbah* our text should read *libbat* not *labbat*, because *libbah* is vocalized like *ginnah* (garden), and the construct of *ginnah* is *ginnat*, not *gannat*. Now, Rabbi Adonim seems to have forgotten the word *gannah* (garden)⁹ or *gannah*. Similarly, the word for heart may be vocalized *libbah* or *labbah*. In the former the construct form is *libbat*, in the latter, *labbat*. The word in our verse follows the paradigm of *labbah*, hence the form *labbat*. in *And as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth* (Is. 61:11).

###### Ibn Ezra on Exodus 3:2:2

[https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/3:2:2](https://torahapp.org/share/book/Ibn%20Ezra%20on%20Exodus/r/3:2:2)


**הסנה.** אמר הגאון כי זה מין קוץ, "ורצון שוכני סנה" (דבר' לג טז) שמים והטעם על השם הנכבד ור' ישועה אמר הכבוד ששכן בסנה ולא דבר נכונה, כי איך יקרא שוכני על רגע אחד, ועוד למה נאמר על גזרת פועל, ואיננו כן עושה שמים וארץ (תה' קכו ח) כי השם הוא עושה תמיד ומעמידם כהגה היוצא מפי אדם ועוד אחר שהזכיר כל מגד הזכיר באחרונה רצון השם, ועוד מה טעם להזכיר זה המלאך, ועוד היה ראוי להיותו שוכני בסנה הידוע, ולפי דעתי כי כל סנה אחד הוא, והוא מין קוץ יבש, וככה הוא בלשון ישמעאל, וככה הר סיני בעבור הסנה וכן פי' ורצון שוכני סנה, רצון שיבקש השוכן במקום הסנה, שהוא דורש ומבקש תמיד שיעשה השם רצונו, וילחלח ארצו שהוא שוכן בה, שהיה מקום יובש וסנה, עד שיהא בא הרווי' והיתה כגן רוה מלוחלח, והודיעו "מתוך הסנה" בה"א הדעת, כי הם דברי משה בכותבו התורה, ובוער מהפעלים היוצאים, כי אש בוערה כמו "אש אוכלה" (דבר' ד כד), והעד "כאש תבער יער" (תה' פג טו) והנה האש שהיה בסנה בוער כל אשר סביביו, כי זה כמו "שלחו באש מקדשך" (תה' עד ז), וככה ההר בוער באש (דבר' ה כ):


THE BUSH. Saadiah Gaon says that *seneh* (bush) is a type of thorn bush. He further explains that the word *seneh* in *And the good will of Him that dwelt* (shokhni) *in the bush* (seneh) (Deut. 33:16) means heaven;¹⁰ has two meanings. It means either a thorn bush or heaven (Filwarg). that is, it refers to God the glorious.¹¹). Rabbi Joshua,¹² on the other hand, says that the verse refers to the glory that dwelt in the bush.¹³ However, Rabbi Joshua spoke incorrectly, for how can God be called “Him that dwelleth in the bush” when he dwelt there for but a moment.¹⁴ Furthermore, why is the word *shokhni* (dwelt) in the *po’el* form?¹⁵ is the present form of words in the *kal*. Since God only revealed Himself once in the bush the perfect *shakhan* (dwelt) should have been used. The word *oseh* (makes) in *Who makes* (oseh) *heaven and earth* (Ps. 121:2) is different,¹⁶ (makes) is a *po’el*, a present form. Now God made heaven and earth at the time of creation. He does not at present make heaven and earth. We thus see that Scripture uses the present form to describe what God did in the past. Now if God is described as making heaven and earth, why can’t He be described as dwelling in the bush? I.E. answers that the two can’t be compared. as God is constantly making and causing heaven and earth to exist in the same manner as speech issues from the mouth of man.¹⁷ (oseh) *heaven and earth*. Isaac Husik in *A History of Medieval Jewish Philosophy*, J.P.S., Philadelphia, 1940, (p. 190) notes that I.E. “seems to favor the idea of eternal creation and maintenance of the universe, the relation of which to God is as the relation of speech to the speaker, which exists only so long as the speaker speaks. The moment he ceases speaking the sounds cease to exist.” Additionally, after mentioning all the *precious things* (Deut. 33:13-16), Scripture concludes with *the good will of God*.¹⁸. If *Him that dwelt in the bush* refers to God, why put the Lord’s blessings last (Krinsky)? Moreover, what reason is there to mention this angel?¹⁹ Furthermore, Scripture should have read, *ba-seneh* (in the bush)²⁰) rather than: And the good will of Him that dwells in a bush (*shokni seneh*). and thereby would have referred to the well-known bush.²¹In my opinion *seneh* (bush) refers to only one thing,²² does not mean a thorn bush or heaven. It has only one meaning. namely, a type of dry thorn bush. This is the case in Arabic.²³. Mount Sinai is so named because this type of bush grew there.²⁴ which grows there. Similarly, its²⁵. interpretation is: and the good will that he who lives in the place of the bush (*seneh*) seeks; that is, a person living in such a place entreats and prays that God do his will and wet the land that he lives in. He prays that God change it from a dry place, a place where the *seneh* grows, to an amply watered place so that it becomes like a wet and well-watered garden. Scripture states that an angel of the Lord appeared *out of the midst of the bush*.²⁶ (the bush) implies a distinctive bush. Since there was as of yet nothing special about the bush, Scripture should have read *seneh* (a bush). It should be noted that J.P.S. translates *ha-seneh* as a bush. However, its literal translation is, the bush. The word *seneh* has the definite article the (*heh*) prefixed to it because these are Moses’ very own words in writing the Torah.²⁷The word *bo’er* (burned) is a transitive verb. The phrase *a burning fire* is similar to *a devouring fire* (Deut. 4:24). *As the fire that burneth* (tivar) *the forest* (Ps. 83:15) is proof of this.²⁸ is transitive. Now the fire that burned in the bush devoured all that was around it. Our verse is similar to *They have set Thy sanctuary on fire* (Ps. 74:7).²⁹ (the bush burned with fire). I.E. believes this should be explained as if written: *ba-seneh bo’er esh* (a fire burnt the bush). He proves that this is the meaning of the clause through Ps. 74:7, which reads: *shilchu va-esh mikdashekha*. The literal meaning is: they have set with fire thy sanctuary. According to I.E. this verse is to be read as if written: *shilchu esh be-mikdashekha* (they have set fire in thy sanctuary) (Filwarg). *While the mountain did burn with fire* (Deut. 5:20) is also similar.³⁰ (while the mountain burned with fire). Now mountains do not burn. Hence I.E. says that the verse should be interpreted as: the mountain consumed its environment with fire. I.E. explains thus because he believes *bo’er* to be a transitive verb.
